THE WAY OF STORY - STUDY NOTES
(Part I: Religion - The Way of Journey and Witness / The Phenomenon of Religion)

INTRODUCTION - DEFINITIONS OF RELIGION
The chapter opens with four definitions of religion to compare:
- Shorter Oxford English Dictionary: religion is the 'recognition on the part of humans of some higher unseen power as having control of their destiny, and as being entitled to obedience, reverence and worship'.
- Ronald J. Wilkins: 'Science and mathematics unravel the problems of the universe; religion responds to the mystery of the universe.'
- Karl Marx: 'Religion is the opium of the masses.'
- Rollo May: religion is 'whatever the individual takes to be his (or her) ultimate concern' - the point where a person is convinced there are values in human existence 'worth living and dying for'.
- Religion is concerned with invisible realities. It is the bridge between the world we see and the unseen.
- A quote by an unknown author: our first task in approaching another people, culture or religion is to 'take off our shoes, for the place we are approaching is holy'. We may tread on another's dream, and we may forget 'that God was there before we arrived'.
- Voltaire: 'If God did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him.'

WHY PEOPLE ARE RELIGIOUS
- Faith is found in every age and region.
- People have always sensed, in the wonders and mysteries of life, someone or something greater than themselves.
- People everywhere ask deep questions: What happens when we die? What is right? What is wrong? Why do bad things happen?
- Religion is a response to this search for ultimate answers.
- Religion offers a relationship with the divine that gives meaning to people's lives and helps make sense of life.
- The belief that life has meaning and worth gives hope in times of pain, confusion and emptiness. It echoes in experiences of love, joy and wonder.
- More than four fifths of the world's population claim some kind of religious belief.
- Religion influences attitudes, values, art, music and literature.
- In most countries over 50 per cent of people follow the same religion or group, e.g. the Greek Orthodox Church in Greece, Mahayana Zen Buddhism in Taiwan, Roman Catholicism in Ireland.

TYPES OF RELIGION - THREE WAYS TO CATEGORISE
The huge variety of religions shows the different ways people respond to the experience of mystery.

1. PROPHETIC AND MYSTICAL RELIGIONS
- Prophets: receive a message from God to pass on to others. This becomes the revealed 'Word of God' - e.g. the Bible for Christians and the Qur'an for Muslims become sacred scripture.
- Mystics: experience union with the divine. The closeness of God is stressed, and followers try to live this experience in daily life. Examples: Buddhism and Hinduism.
- In reality all major world religions have both prophetic and mystical elements, but stress one more.
- In Islam the prophetic element is stronger. In Hinduism the mystical is stronger.
- Ninian Smart, the renowned historian of religions, says that in Christianity the balance between prophetic and mystical is about equal.

2. CONCEPT OF DEITY (how a religion sees God)
- Concept of deity: the way a religion understands God or the divine.
- Polytheistic: belief in many gods. Examples: primal religions and popular Hinduism.
- Pantheistic: the divine is present in all things. Examples: Mahayana Buddhism and some forms of Hinduism.
- Monotheistic: one God who rules over all. Examples: Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

3. ANCESTRY
- Ancestry: tracing which religions came out of other religions.
- A timeline (2500 BCE to 2000 CE) shows this. E.g. Christianity and Islam emerged out of Judaism.
- Timeline items include ancient civilisations (Olmec, Mayan, Aztec, Inca, Sumerian, Akkadian, Babylonian, Assyrian, Canaanite, Hittite, Egypt, Persian, Minoan, Mycenaean, Greek city states, Byzantine, Roman Republic, Northern European, Chinese dynasties) and religions (Hinduism, Jainism, Buddhism, Sikhism, Zoroastrianism, Parsis, Ancient Israel, Christianity, Islam, Confucianism, Taoism, Shinto, Baha'i).

DIMENSIONS OF RELIGION
- Dimensions of religion: the common elements found in all the major world religions.
- These common elements can be used to describe and understand religion as a worldwide phenomenon.

WORLDWIDE DISTRIBUTION OF RELIGION
- CHRISTIANITY: the world's largest religion. 2.1 billion followers, over 33 per cent of the world population. Main faith in North and South America and Eastern and Western Europe. Catholicism is the largest denomination with 1.1 billion. Anglican Communion: 80 million.
- ISLAM: almost 1.3 billion, 22 per cent of the world. Most Middle East countries and many in North Africa are mainly Muslim.
- HINDUISM: third largest, 14 per cent, 900 million, mainly in India, Nepal and Mauritius.
- BUDDHISM: about 376 million, in South-East Asia and China, despite political oppression.
- TAOISM: 20 million, mainly China and Taiwan.
- SIKHISM: 22 million, 20 million in India, the majority in the State of Punjab.
- JUDAISM: 14 million, almost 6 million in the USA and 4.7 million in Israel.
- BAHA'ISM: 7 million, 1.8 million in Africa.
- CONFUCIANISM: 6 million, 4 million in Asia and 1.8 million in South Korea.

RELIGION IN EUROPE
- Broad division: Catholic Southern Europe and Protestant Northern Europe.
- Spain and Italy: Roman Catholic Church keeps an important social position.
- Five Scandinavian countries: Protestant national state churches.
- Germany: Protestant and Roman Catholic churches equal in strength.
- England and Wales: highly secularised, low attendance. Protestant church membership fell from 22 per cent in 1900 to 6 per cent in 2000.
- Formal church attendance across Europe fell to 25 per cent (from 30 per cent once a month in 1990).
- European Values Study (EVS, 2000): Europeans have become 'more pronounced in their beliefs'. Only 5 per cent say they are atheists. Acceptance of contraception, abortion, divorce, homosexuality and euthanasia varies widely - a more permissive climate is developing. Acceptance of joyriding, tax evasion, bribery and benefit abuse is much lower.
- Ireland 2003: weekly church attendance 59 per cent in the twenty-six counties, 49 per cent in Northern Ireland.
- Scotland: large numbers in the Presbyterian tradition.
- Migration in the twentieth century means people live alongside other faiths (sometimes leading to conversion).
- Large Muslim communities in Britain, Germany and Holland. Significant Sikh and Hindu communities in England.
- House Church Movement: growing weekly gatherings of prayer and witness. These groups hold to the main Christian beliefs (the deity of Jesus Christ and his bodily resurrection). It shows people still search for spiritual growth.

FAITH BRINGS OUT THE BEST AND WORST IN PEOPLE
- It has inspired heroic unselfishness, but for others it led to superiority and exclusivity.
- It has brought peace to many, but has been a cause of war for others.
- People live by it, and some die for it.
- It has inspired poetry, literature, music, liturgies and contemplation.
- Many draw strength from it in suffering, while others use it to spread suspicion, prejudice and hatred.
- For most, being touched by the divine means ordinary life is transcended - the mundane is made sacred - life is holy.

RELIGIOUS TRADITIONS IN IRELAND
- Ireland as a whole: 75 per cent Roman Catholic, 7 per cent Church of Ireland (Anglican), 6 per cent Presbyterian.
- Both the Church of Ireland and the Roman Catholic Church trace their origins to St Patrick and the Celtic Church, founded some time in the fifth century.
- Celtic Christianity and Roman Catholicism became one. In the Middle Ages Irish religion was exclusively Catholic.
- The Reformation began in Europe in the sixteenth century.
- 1542: Henry VIII declared he and his heirs would be 'Kings of Ireland'.
- James I (1603-25) 'planted' English Anglican and Scottish Presbyterian settlers in six counties of Ulster - the Plantation of Ulster.
- Under British rule, religious and political differences grew, with legitimate Catholic grievances over land and discrimination.
- The 1916 Rising and the War of Independence led to the Anglo-Irish Treaty and partition in 1921 into Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland.
- Partition symbolises a deeper partition in the 'Irish' mind over religion.
- About 8 per cent profess no religion. The rest: smaller Protestant denominations, Muslims, Jews, Buddhists and New Religious Movements.

RELIGIOUS TRENDS IN IRELAND
- Causes of change: rising wealth and education, scientific and technological progress, challenges to traditional authority, more democracy and political co-operation.
- Four trends: Secularism and Secularisation; Religion and the Environment; Ecumenism; Celtic Spirituality.

SECULARISM
- Secularism: a philosophy of life limited to the present here-and-now materialist culture.
- Rooted in the rise of secular humanism in the Renaissance, strengthened by scientific thought.
- In the Enlightenment science became more influential than religion as it challenged religious beliefs and church authority.
- Secularism denies the influence of religion. There is no 'other worldly' or transcendent source of meaning. Only what can be proven matters.
- Latin 'saeculum' means 'the present age'.

SECULARISATION
- Secularisation: not a philosophy but a movement in culture that focuses on nature and science and their benefits to humankind.
- A secularised culture does not look to 'other-worldly' meaning and rejects the role of religion in society.
- A secularised society shows declining interest in religion; religious structures have little influence on ethical, economic or social thought.
- Communist countries made systematic efforts to wipe out organised religion, but these seem to have failed.

EOIN G. CASSIDY - 'MODERNITY AND RELIGION IN IRELAND'
- Looks at how modernity affected religious beliefs, values and practice in Ireland 1980-2000.
- Modernity: an umbrella term for many cultural developments in Europe over the past two hundred years, including secularisation.
- Uses the 1991 and 1998 International Social Survey Programme (ISSP) and the 1981, 1990 and 1999 European Values Study (EVS).
- Signs of secularisation would be: less affiliation to mainstream religions, vague belief in God, falling attendance, decline in doctrinal and ethical beliefs.
- 8 per cent of the Irish can be identified as 'secularists' (1999 EVS), up from 2.5 per cent (1981 EVS) - low compared to Europe.
- 96 per cent belief in God (EVS). Cassidy concludes there is resistance to secularisation in Ireland.
- BUT a decline in following Catholic moral teaching (abortion, premarital sex, same-sex relations) suggests 'the influence of a secularist ethos'.
- Church influence is weaker among the 18-26/28 age group - secularist tendencies among young adults.

PETER BERGER - THE SACRED CANOPY
- Defines secularisation as a 'process by which sectors of society and culture are removed from the domination of religious institutions and symbols'.
- Sectors: economics, science and technology, politics, media and education.
- Religion is now a personal commitment, not a framework for community or social development.

OTHER QUOTES ON SECULARISATION
- Harold Kushner: 'When we have succeeded in putting out all the sacred fires, where will we turn for warmth and light?'
- C.M. Gay: secularisation is not likely to be 'the last word', but Western societies will probably never again be under a single 'sacred canopy' of religious meaning.
- Conclusion: a secular, pluralistic society gives religious people chances to be true to their faith. Religious tradition, open to the future, offers a stable basis for dialogue with the modern world.

RELIGION AND THE ENVIRONMENT - A GLOBAL ETHIC
- Ecological crisis: the ongoing devastation of the natural world.
- Causes: technological, political, economic, industrial, social development of indigenous peoples.
- Shared religious insight: the earth is sacred and humans are stewards of creation. This can lead to shared solutions.
- Interdependence of human life and the natural world.
- Threats: pollution, deforestation, erosion, disturbance of the atmosphere, extinction of tens of thousands of species - unsustainable.
- Judaism, Christianity, Islam: God the Creator and the goodness of creation mean humans must care for the earth.
- Exodus 23:10: let the land rest (lie fallow) one year in seven.
- Psalms 19 and 148: poetic praise of the beauty of the heavens and God's glory - wonder leads to respect and stewardship, not ownership.
- Stewardship vs ownership: caring for the earth on God's behalf rather than owning it.
- Christianity: belief in the incarnation sees all human life as good and sacred. The Eucharist uses bread and wine, 'fruit of the earth and of the vine, work of human hands' - the holiness of ordinary things.
- Islam: humans are Caliph - God's trustee on earth.
- Hinduism: Hindus belong to the world and do not own it. All creation is a manifestation of God, not to be exploited.
- Father Sean McDonagh on 'living water': Christians need a positive theology of the oceans. Water for baptism should be truly 'living water', not merely industrial water or H2O. We need to respect water like Jesus did.
- Elizabeth Barrett Browning: 'Earth is crammed with heaven, and every common bush afire with God.'

ECUMENISM - A MODERN CHRISTIAN MOVEMENT FOR UNITY
- John 17:21: '...that they may all be one. As you, Father, are in me and I am in you, may they also be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.'
- Ecumenism: the movement for unity among Christian churches, a response to this prayer of Jesus.
- Comes from three Greek words: Oikos (a family, people or nation); Oikoumene (the whole community or whole inhabited world); Oikoumenikos (open to the whole world or related).
- Used fifteen times in the New Testament meaning 'the whole world'. Later it referred to the 'People of God'.
- In the last one hundred years it has meant the search for unity among Christian churches.
- Locally: interdenominational prayer groups, social projects, community initiatives.
- Formally: inter-church conferences, documents and agreements; unity within diversity.
- Christians are separated by doctrine, worship and history but share spiritual values, art and music.
- World Council of Churches: officially formed 1948, roots in late nineteenth century.
- 1908: two Anglicans founded the Church Unity Octave - an annual week of prayer for Christian unity, still observed.
- WCC members: Anglicans, Baptists, Lutherans, Friends, Orthodox, Methodists, Reformed and Pentecostal churches. The Roman Catholic Church is not a member but works with it on social collaboration and common witness.
- Ireland: the Irish Council of Churches and the Catholic Commission for Justice and Peace jointly promote peace and reconciliation in Northern Ireland (Inter-Church Committee, peace education programmes for schools).
- Christian Renewal Centre, Rostrevor, Co. Down: founded 1974 by Rev. Cecil Kerr.
- Corrymeela Community: set up 1965 by Presbyterian chaplain Ray Davey.
- Also mentioned: Ballymacscanlon Inter-Church Conference; Irish School of Ecumenics, established 1970.

CELTIC CHRISTIANITY - A EUROPEAN HERITAGE
- Celtic Christianity: the Christian spirituality of fifth-century Britain and Ireland, now enjoying renewed interest.
- Offers ways of life, work and worship different from mainstream practice; sees religion as part of everyday life.
- D.E. Meek: since 1980 Celtic spirituality has been reconstructed to make up for perceived failures of orthodox Christianity. It is environmentally friendly, bridges the Cartesian split between spirit and matter, is sympathetic to non-Christian culture (can accommodate pagan or primal practices, e.g. Celtic saints absorbing druidic teaching), non-aggressive in evangelising, ecumenical, eclectic and syncretic, and open to visions and spiritual 'impressions'.
- For the Celts the 'other world' was as near as this world. Everything had an underlying unity; each person was part of the cosmic whole.
- God's immanence: God's presence in the world, living care and protection. All of life was an encounter with God.
- Unity of sacred and profane is a key inspiring element.
- John O'Donohue: his writing and talks show growing interest. He says the Celtic mind was 'neither discursive nor systematic' and 'not burdened by dualism'. It did not separate visible from invisible, time from eternity, human from divine. Their 'ontological friendship' embraced nature, divinity, underworld and human world as one. This unifying friendship is 'the Celtic gift'.
- Lorica: an encompassing protection prayer of the Christian Celts, e.g. St Patrick's Breastplate: 'I pray the protection of Christ to clothe me, Christ to enfold me, To surround me and guard me this day and every day...'

KEY TERMS
- Prophetic and mystical religions; Concept of deity; Ancestry; Dimensions of religion; Secularism; Secularisation; Ecological crisis; Ecumenism; Celtic Christianity.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between a prophetic and a mystical religion.
rows.model_answer: In a prophetic religion a prophet receives a message from God to pass on, which becomes the revealed Word of God, such as the Bible or the Qur'an. In a mystical religion followers experience union with the divine and stress God's closeness, as in Buddhism and Hinduism. All major religions have both elements, but stress one more.

rows.prompt: Name and explain the three ways of describing a religion's concept of deity.
rows.model_answer: Polytheistic religions believe in many gods, e.g. primal religions and popular Hinduism. Pantheistic religions see the divine in all things, e.g. Mahayana Buddhism. Monotheistic religions believe in one God who rules over all, e.g. Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between secularism and secularisation.
rows.model_answer: Secularism is a philosophy of life limited to the here-and-now material world; it denies any transcendent source of meaning and says only what can be proven matters. Secularisation is not a philosophy but a movement in culture that focuses on science and nature. A secularised society shows declining interest in religion and religion has little influence on its ethical, economic or social life.

rows.prompt: How does Peter Berger define secularisation, and which sectors does he name?
rows.model_answer: In The Sacred Canopy Berger defines secularisation as the process by which sectors of society and culture are removed from the domination of religious institutions and symbols. He names economics, science and technology, politics, media and education. He says religion is now a personal commitment rather than a framework for society.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between stewardship and ownership of the earth.
rows.model_answer: Ownership means treating the earth as ours to use as we like. Stewardship means caring for the earth on God's behalf because it is sacred and belongs to God. Religions such as Judaism, Christianity and Islam teach that humans are stewards or trustees of creation, and Hindus say they belong to the world rather than own it.

rows.prompt: What is ecumenism and where does the word come from?
rows.model_answer: Ecumenism is the movement for unity among Christian churches, a response to Jesus' prayer 'that they may all be one' (John 17:21). The word comes from Greek: oikos (a family, people or nation), oikoumene (the whole inhabited world) and oikoumenikos (open to the whole world).

rows.prompt: Name two ecumenical centres in Ireland and who founded them.
rows.model_answer: The Corrymeela Community was set up in 1965 by Presbyterian chaplain Ray Davey. The Christian Renewal Centre in Rostrevor, Co. Down, was established in 1974 by Rev. Cecil Kerr. Both work to build bridges of peace and unity between Christians.

rows.prompt: What is 'the Celtic gift' according to John O'Donohue?
rows.model_answer: O'Donohue says the Celtic mind was not burdened by dualism: it did not separate the visible from the invisible, time from eternity or human from divine. The Celts saw nature, divinity, underworld and human world as one, in an 'ontological friendship'. This unifying friendship is the Celtic gift to our divided world.

rows.prompt: Outline the evidence for and against the secularisation of Irish society, with reference to research you have studied.
rows.model_answer: Secularisation is a movement in culture where religion loses its influence on society. Eoin G. Cassidy, in 'Modernity and Religion in Ireland', studied the ISSP (1991, 1998) and EVS (1981, 1990, 1999) surveys. Against secularisation: belief in God in Ireland was 96 per cent, and only 8 per cent could be called 'secularists' - low compared to other European countries. Weekly church attendance in 2003 was still 59 per cent in the twenty-six counties and 49 per cent in Northern Ireland. Cassidy therefore saw a resistance to secularisation. For secularisation: the number of secularists rose from 2.5 per cent in 1981 to 8 per cent in 1999. There is also a decline in acceptance of Catholic moral teaching on abortion, premarital sex and same-sex relations, which Cassidy says reflects 'the influence of a secularist ethos'. This is strongest among young adults aged 18-26/28. Peter Berger in The Sacred Canopy argues that sectors such as economics, politics, media and education have been removed from religious control, so that religion is now a personal commitment. Overall, belief remains strong in Ireland but its influence on moral and social life is weakening.

rows.prompt: Describe two different ways of categorising world religions. Give examples in each case.
rows.model_answer: One way is to distinguish between prophetic and mystical religions. In prophetic religions a prophet receives a message from God to pass on, which becomes the revealed Word of God, such as the Bible for Christians and the Qur'an for Muslims. In mystical religions, such as Buddhism and Hinduism, followers experience union with the divine and try to live that closeness in daily life. All major religions have both elements: Islam is mainly prophetic, Hinduism mainly mystical, and Ninian Smart says Christianity is about equally balanced. A second way is by concept of deity. Polytheistic religions believe in many gods, such as primal religions and popular Hinduism. Pantheistic religions see the divine as present in all things, such as Mahayana Buddhism and some forms of Hinduism. Monotheistic religions, Judaism, Christianity and Islam, believe in one God who rules over all. A third way is ancestry, tracing which religions grew out of others, such as Christianity and Islam emerging from Judaism.

Many religions share the insight that the earth is sacred and humans are its stewards, which can lead to shared solutions. rows.prompt: Explain why Celtic spirituality appeals to many people today.
rows.model_answer: Celtic Christianity is the spirituality of fifth-century Britain and Ireland, which has had renewed interest in recent years. It offers ways of life, work and worship that are refreshingly different from mainstream practice and sees religion as part of everyday life. For the Celts the 'other world' was as near as this world, everything had an underlying unity and each person was part of the cosmic whole. They had a strong sense of God's immanence - God's presence, care and protection in all of life - so all living was an encounter with God. This unity of sacred and profane inspires people today. This is seen in Lorica prayers such as St Patrick's Breastplate: 'Christ to enfold me, to surround me and guard me'. D.E. Meek says that since 1980 it has been rebuilt to make up for perceived failures of orthodox Christianity: it is environmentally friendly, bridges the split between spirit and matter, is open to other cultures, non-aggressive and ecumenical. John O'Donohue says the Celtic mind was not burdened by dualism; its 'ontological friendship' between nature, divinity and humans is 'the Celtic gift' to our divided world.
